newsitem.title: USA: EchoStar stock soars on News Corp. TV alliance.
newsitem.headline: EchoStar stock soars on News Corp. TV alliance.

text.p: The stock of EchoStar Communications Corp. soared Tuesday, a day after the satellite TV company set an alliance with News Corp. to offer direct-broadcast satellite television service to compete with cable providers.
Industry analysts said the venture announced on Monday would present a formidable challenge to the cable TV industry, and investors who were clearly worried sent cable stocks lower.

Under the deal, Rupert Murdoch's News Corp., which owns the Fox television network, would contribute satellites, cash and other assets worth $1 billion from its American Sky Broadcasting unit for a 50 percent stake in EchoStar.
The direct-broadcast venture would offer as many as 500 channels of digital TV, Internet services and local broadcast TV signals to markets across the United States.
EchoStar jumped $8.75 to $26.75 on Nasdaq market and News Corp. stock added 62.5 cents to $21.875 on the New York Stock Exchange.
Tele-Communications Inc. class A stock fell $1 to $13 on Nasdaq, and Cox Communications shares lost $1.25 to $21.75 on the NYSE.

"A consolidated satellite industry is certainly more competitive to cable," said Bob Scherman, editor and publisher of Satellite Business News magazine. "It's more focused marketing. It's less confusion within the industry."
"If you're Primestar or DirecTV, you've got to be more concerned than you were yesterday," senior analyst John Mansell of Paul Kagan Associates said.

DirecTV, owned by General Motors Corp.'s Hughes Electronics and AT&T Corp., and Primestar, owned by a host of cable television operators, have the largest block of the direct-broadcast satellite industry's 4.5 million subscribers, with EchoStar distantly behind.
There are about 64 million cable television subscribers in the United States.

While the new venture faces formidable hurdles, News Corp. has built its Fox network into a strong fourth competitor in the broadcast industry, and News Corp. brings capital sorely needed by EchoStar, the analysts said.
"It now has a little bit more financial might to make it more of a competitive threat," A.G. Edwards analyst James Jungjohann said of Echostar.
But he and others said that Primestar and DirecTV already have a strong lead in the direct broadcast satellite industry.
"The low hanging fruit is probably gone," Jungjohann said. "Rupert is somewhat late to the party but they're going to make a big bang."
Some analysts said regulators might object to the deal but others said that was probably not a major concern.
A regulatory official said the government's role would depend on what the details looked like.

"It's likely they'll need to come to us. We'll have to wait to see what they file and how the deal is structured," said one official with the Federal Communications Commission who requested anonymity.

MCI Communications Corp., a partner in American Sky Broadcasting, will acquire part of News Corp.'s stake in the venture, leaving News Corp. with 40 percent. MCI would hold a 10 percent stake and EchoStar 50 percent of the venture.
The TV service, to be operated using News Corp.'s Sky brand name, is scheduled to begin delivering programmes to U.S. households early next year.
Unlike rival direct satellite providers, which are precluded from offering local programmes, Sky expects to be able to offer both local programmes and premium channels.

At first, the local programmes will be available to 50 percent of American households, but by the end of next year the service area will be increased to 75 percent, creating a substantial competitor to cable operators and other satellite services, the officials said.
News Corp. also controls British Sky Broadcasting, or BSkyB, Britain's leading pay-TV provider, and has a satellite TV joint venture in Japan, JSkyB, that is expected to begin full service next year.
